title: Eruption of Samalas volcano
summary: Samalas, part of the Rinjani volcanic complex on Lombok, Indonesia, erupted in 1257 (some sources say 1258), ejecting about 40 cubic kilometres of rock and leaving a caldera about 6.5 by 8 km. Polar ice shows the largest sulfate peak in 2,300 years, around 1259; the volcano was identified as the source in 2013.

uncertainty.note: Discover gives 1257 or 1258; the CNRS article says the volcano began to reawaken in 1257 and puts the ice sulfate peak around 1259.

as_recorded.value: An eruption that occurred in 1257 or 1258 A.D.

where.modern_name: Segara Anak caldera, Rinjani volcanic complex, Lombok, Indonesia
where.historical_name: Samalas volcano, ancestral part of the Rinjani complex, Lombok (island of Lombok, Indonesia)

importance.justification: The eruption behind the largest polar-ice sulfate peak of the past 2,300 years, described as having disrupted the world's climate in the Middle Ages.

reviewer_note: Pinned at the Segara Anak lake in the caldera, which Discover names as the caldera formed by the 1257 eruption. Neither source ties the eruption to the Little Ice Age, so no link to 1300-little-ice-age is made. Volume stated as 35-40 km3 (Discover) and about 40 km3 (CNRS); the 2013 PNAS paper itself was not opened.
